title: Rabies, Food Safety, and Why Vietnam's Unregulated Dog Trade Is a Public Health Crisis
excerpt: Vietnam loses ₫600 billion annually to rabies, yet 100% of dog slaughterhouses operate illegally with zero food safety oversight. New April 2026 raids expose the health toll—and why 95% of Vietnamese want it stopped.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam's dog meat trade isn't just an animal welfare issue—it's a public health emergency. Unregulated slaughterhouses are directly linked to rabies transmission, unsafe food handling, and rampant pet theft networks. Vietnam spends ₫600 billion annually combating rabies—a disease with a near-100% fatality rate once symptoms appear. Yet authorities only recently intensified enforcement, and 95% of Vietnamese citizens support ending the trade entirely.

Key Findings

Rabies Risk Hidden in Vietnam's Unregulated Slaughterhouses

According to PGS.TS Bùi Hoài Sơn, slaughtering unknown-source dogs poses direct rabies exposure risk to workers and consumers. Vietnam currently records 70–90 rabies deaths annually, with 2026 showing multiple fatalities across Tây Ninh (4 cases), Đà Nẵng (7 outbreaks), and Ho Chi Minh City. The economic toll is staggering: Vietnam loses ₫600 billion per year to rabies prevention and treatment. The trade perpetuates this crisis because only 50% of Vietnam's estimated 7 million dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies—well below the 80% threshold needed for herd immunity.

The April 2026 Ho Chi Minh City raids underscore this danger. Authorities discovered two illegal slaughterhouses with 12 live dogs, 15 kg of dog meat, 32 live cats, and 112 kg of frozen organs—sourced from multiple provinces with no veterinary inspection certificates. Workers in such facilities face direct exposure during slaughter and processing, with no biosecurity protocols.

Zero Food Safety Standards in Vietnam's Dog Meat Supply Chain

The April 13, 2026 raids reveal the scale of food safety violations. Both Ho Chi Minh City facilities operated without documentation of origin, veterinary inspection, or disease screening; both were shut down and their products destroyed. There are zero registered dog meat slaughterhouses in Vietnam—meaning the entire supply chain is unregulated. Dogs sourced from theft rings or unknown origins carry unpredictable disease burdens. Consumers have no way to verify if meat is contaminated with E. coli, Salmonella, or other pathogens commonly found in improperly handled animal products.

Pet Theft Networks Feed the Unregulated Trade, Fueling Public Health Risks

In Q1 2026 alone, Ho Chi Minh City police arrested 31 individuals for pet theft across 12 separate incidents, with stolen dogs often ending up in the meat supply chain. Thieves use sophisticated tactics—posing as dog walkers or using cloth sacks to capture animals on quiet nighttime streets—then sell them to slaughterhouses through informal networks. Stolen family pets have unknown vaccination histories and health records, making them a direct rabies vector. When these animals reach slaughterhouses, they bypass any possibility of disease screening.

Yet despite this crisis, a 2021 FOUR PAWS survey found 95% of Vietnamese believe dog and cat meat consumption is not part of Vietnamese culture, and 88% support a complete trade ban. This is not a cultural tradition; it is a public health hazard that the vast majority of Vietnamese citizens reject.

Hanoi and HCM Escalate Enforcement—But National Ban Remains Absent

Hanoi's government issued Directive 4170/UBND-KT mandating mandatory rabies vaccination, pet registration, and administrative penalties for unvaccinated animals roaming public spaces. Ho Chi Minh City has launched surprise raids targeting illegal slaughterhouses. But Vietnam still lacks a national ban on dog meat trade—a legislative gap that allows the unregulated supply chain to persist. The Ministry of Agriculture and Environment has outlined a roadmap to phase out the trade by 2030, but enforcement remains inconsistent across provinces.

Also Worth Noting

  • Vaccination Gap Widening Despite Increased Outbreaks — Despite a 10% increase in rabies vaccination and 30% increase in serum use in late 2025, only 50% of Vietnam's 7 million dogs and cats are protected, leaving the population vulnerable to endemic transmission.
  • Regional Trade Estimates Show Scale of Cross-Border Risk — An estimated 10 million dogs and cats are slaughtered annually across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Indonesia, multiplying opportunities for disease spillover and cross-border contamination.
  • One-Year Incubation Periods Mean Delayed Diagnosis and Death — A 55-year-old Tây Ninh resident died in 2026 from a dog bite sustained nearly one year earlier, after failing to complete the post-exposure vaccine protocol—a reminder that rabies prevention requires immediate action.
  • Slaughterhouses Operate in Residential Areas, Increasing Community Exposure — Both April 2026 raids targeted facilities within crowded market zones and residential neighborhoods, putting families and workers at direct risk of occupational or incidental rabies exposure.
  • 95% Vietnamese Support Ending Trade—Policy Must Catch Up — The massive gap between public opinion and national law shows that enforcement and legislation, not culture, are the barriers to ending this public health crisis.

Take Action: This is not about imposing values—it is about protecting public health and honoring what the Vietnamese people have already decided. Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030, backed by community safety, food security, and the will of 95% of Vietnamese citizens.
